title: Does funding from a grant disqualify me from R&D tax credits?
description: Receiving a grant does not automatically disqualify a U.S. business from the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41.
summary: Receiving a grant does not automatically disqualify a U.S. business from the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41. Grant funding triggers the funded-research exclusion only to the extent research is funded: eligibility depends on whether the business retains substantial rights in the results and whether payment is contingent on research success, with remaining qualified expenses still claimable.

body.text: Receiving a grant does not automatically disqualify a U.S. business from the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41. Grant funding triggers the funded-research exclusion only to the extent research is funded: eligibility depends on whether the business retains substantial rights in the results and whether payment is contingent on research success, with remaining qualified expenses still claimable.
1. The short answer

No. Receiving a grant does not disqualify a business from the research credit outright. What a grant does do is trigger the funded-research exclusion. Under IRC §41(d)(4)(H), qualified research does not include "Any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)." The words "to the extent" matter. The exclusion removes the funded portion of the research. It does not remove the whole project, and it does not remove the taxpayer's other, unrelated research from the credit computation.

Courts describe the purpose in similar terms: when a contractor performs research for a customer, both parties could otherwise claim the same expenses (the contractor as in-house research expenses, the customer as contract research expenses), and the funded-research rules decide which of them, if either, is entitled to the credit. The same logic applies when the "customer" is a government agency or a private foundation awarding a grant.

The practical consequence for a grant recipient is that the analysis is never "grant or no grant." It is a three-part inquiry: (1) does the grant agreement leave the business with substantial rights in the research results; (2) is any payment under the agreement contingent on the success of the research; and (3) if the research is funded only in part, how much of the funding must be charged against the expenses that would otherwise qualify. Sections 2 through 4 below walk through each part.

items: The credit is permanent. Pub. L. 114-113 (the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015, enacted as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016), §121, struck the former termination date in §41(h) and made the credit permanent. Before that, the credit had expired and been retroactively extended many times since its original enactment in 1981.
The 2014 usage figures (more than $12.5 billion claimed on nearly 18,000 corporate returns). Even if accurate, these figures are now more than a decade old and do not describe current claim volumes.

body.text: 2. The legal test: when is grant-funded research "funded"?
2.1 Where the rule lives

The statute is IRC §41(d)(4)(H). The current regulation, Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(9), repeats the exclusion and states: "To determine the extent to which research is so funded, § 1.41-4A(d) applies." The working rules are therefore in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d). The Eighth Circuit quoted this exact cross-reference in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), confirming that courts treat §1.41-4A(d) as the operative definition of "funded."

Under §1.41-4A(d)(1), every agreement between the taxpayer doing the research and other persons is taken into account, not only formal research contracts. A grant agreement, its payment terms, its reporting and milestone provisions, and its intellectual-property clauses all form part of the analysis. For a federal grant, that typically includes the award notice, the agency's general terms and conditions incorporated by reference, and any data-rights or patent-rights clauses that apply to the program.

Update – the regulations survive a Loper Bright challenge. After the Supreme Court's 2024 decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which ended Chevron deference, taxpayers began challenging the funded-research regulations. In Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026), as summarized by KPMG, the Tax Court rejected a Loper Bright challenge and upheld Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d). Grant recipients should therefore continue to assume the regulatory tests described below govern their claims.
2.2 Test 1: economic risk (is payment contingent on success?)

The regulation does not use the phrase "economic risk." It asks whether payment is contingent on the research succeeding. Under §1.41-4A(d)(1), amounts that are payable only if the research succeeds are treated as paid for the product or result, so they are not funding. The IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) frames the question the same way: if payment is not contingent on success, the research is treated as funded.

The Tax Adviser (Sweigart, June 2024) likewise describes the funded-research inquiry as a two-pronged analysis of whether the taxpayer bears economic risk tied to the success of the research and whether it retains substantial rights in the results.

The regulatory test is narrower. It looks at whether payment depends on the research succeeding. A payment can be uncertain for other reasons (for example, the funder's creditworthiness, a termination-for-convenience clause, or general project risk) and still not be contingent on research success.

They are consistent with the regulation: a cost-reimbursement grant, which is the standard structure for most federal research grants, pays for allowable costs as they are incurred whether or not the research works, and is therefore ordinarily "funding" under §1.41-4A(d)(1).

Case law. The full citation is Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 23-1523, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024), affirming a Tax Court summary judgment for the IRS. The taxpayer, a structural engineering firm, claimed roughly $190,000 in credits. The Eighth Circuit held that its research was funded because none of its contracts expressly or by clear implication made payment contingent on the success of the research. The court acknowledged that the firm's fixed-price contracts carried a general economic risk of investing resources without a commitment to be paid, but held that general risk is not the same as payment contingent on research success.

The Eighth Circuit relied in turn on United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. Nov. 13, 2023), which rejected the argument that the "risky" nature of fixed-price contracts made them per se unfunded, and held that payments not contingent on research success left the research funded. It also contrasted Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1996), where the contract's detailed technical specifications meant the taxpayer had to succeed at each step to be paid, so the research was not funded.

Update – Smith v. Commissioner (2026). In Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026), an architectural firm's research was held partially funded. According to KPMG's summary, for the projects where the firm kept substantial rights, payments tied to monthly progress or phase completion were not contingent on success; the court followed Meyer, Borgman & Johnson in requiring that success be measurable under specific, detailed contract criteria. For grant recipients, the lesson carries over directly: grant disbursements tied to time periods, progress reports, or completion of a work phase, rather than to the research actually succeeding, will ordinarily be treated as funding.
2.3 Test 2: substantial rights

Under §1.41-4A(d)(2), if the taxpayer retains no substantial rights in the research, the research is treated as fully funded and none of its expenses are qualified research expenses (QREs). If, in addition, payment is contingent on success, neither party may claim the expenses. Under §1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), a taxpayer that must pay for the right to use the results does not retain substantial rights. Incidental benefits, such as the experience the taxpayer's staff gains from doing the work, do not count as substantial rights.
The Fifth Circuit in Grigsby described the regulations the same way: research is funded if the researcher retains no substantial rights, or if payment is not contingent on the research's success.

Commentary in The Tax Adviser (Sweigart, June 2024) adds that in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), non-exclusive rights to use the results without paying the government were enough. That is directly relevant to many federally funded projects, where the government takes a license but the performer keeps the right to use the technology. The article also reports that taxpayers lost in Tangel and Grigsby because they could not show they retained rights.

items: Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1 (Jan. 11, 2021). Judge Lauber granted the IRS partial summary judgment on one project, holding that the research performed by Enercon Engineering (an S corporation whose shareholders claimed the flow-through credit) was 100% funded by its customer because Enercon did not retain substantial rights under the agreement.

United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023). The Fifth Circuit held that three of four sample projects performed by Cajun Industries failed the substantial-rights standard, because each contract assigned ownership of the work product and research results to the customer, and that the fourth was funded because payment was not contingent on success.

body.text: In Smith (2026), two of the six sample projects failed the substantial-rights step because the contracts transferred copyright, made project data the client's "absolute property," and required express prior written approval before the firm could reuse project information. Grant agreements that vest all data and intellectual property in the funder, or that require the recipient to obtain permission (or pay) to use its own results, raise the same risk.

According to the Tax Adviser article, Notice 2023-63 (with Notice 2024-12 defining an "SRE product right") sets rules for research providers under §174. Notice 2023-63 itself states that it "is not intended to change the rules for determining eligibility for or computation of the research credit under § 41." Its §174 test also differs: it focuses on legally protectable end products, while §41 rights can attach to underlying technological information. The notices are parallel guidance, not an amendment of the §41 test. Note also that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21) added new IRC §174A, which, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, lets domestic research expenditures be deducted currently or, by election, amortized over at least 60 months (IRS Instructions for Form 6765, Rev. 12/2025). That change affects the deduction side of research costs; it does not amend the §41(d)(4)(H) funded-research exclusion.
2.4 Analysis: contract language decides the outcome

It is consistent with the regulation's instruction to review all agreements and with the cases above, where results turned on payment and IP clauses. The 2024–2026 decisions strengthen the point: in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Smith, the taxpayers lost not because their work lacked technical risk, but because their agreements did not expressly tie payment to research success or preserve their rights in the results.

For a grant recipient, the practical checklist that follows from the regulation and the cases is: (1) identify every document that forms the agreement; (2) locate the clauses that govern ownership of, and the recipient's right to use, data, inventions, and other results; (3) locate the clauses that govern when and why money is paid, and whether any payment can be withheld or refunded if the research fails; and (4) decide, before signing where possible, whether the business intends to claim the credit for any portion of the work.
3. SBIR and STTR grants
3.1 Program facts checked

items: Phases. The Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs use a three-phase structure: Phase I (feasibility and proof of concept), Phase II (full research and development effort), and Phase III (commercialization funded by non-SBIR/STTR money).
STTR work split. The small business must perform at least 40% of the work and the partner research institution at least 30%.
STTR IP agreement. ADP's article states that STTR partners must have a formal agreement covering IP rights, follow-on research, and commercialization.

Currency update. SBIR/STTR statutory authority expired on September 30, 2025. From October 1, 2025 until reauthorization, agencies could not issue new SBIR or STTR solicitations or obligate new awards. On April 13, 2026, the President signed the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (S. 3971), enacted as Pub. L. 119-83, after the Senate passed it on March 3, 2026 and the House on March 17, 2026 (345–41). The Act reauthorizes both programs through September 30, 2031, allows agencies to carry unobligated fiscal year 2026 funds into fiscal year 2027, and adds a new post-Phase II "Strategic Breakthrough" award category, expanded foreign-risk screening, and per-firm proposal caps beginning in fiscal year 2027 (per the Congressional Research Service and law-firm summaries). Agencies have resumed solicitations. Awards made before the lapse were not affected. None of these program changes alters the federal tax treatment of SBIR/STTR funding, which continues to be governed by IRC §41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d).

body.text: 3.2 How the exclusion maps onto each phase (analysis)

No IRS ruling sets phase-specific rules for SBIR or STTR awards. Each award still has to be tested under §1.41-4A(d) on its own terms: first for substantial rights, then for whether payment is contingent on success, then (if the research is only partly funded) for allocation.

cells: Phase I (feasibility)
Often fully covered by the award and paid regardless of outcome, so frequently excluded in full.

Plausible under the contingency test, but this is a generalization. The award terms control. Where the award is a grant or cost-reimbursement contract that pays for allowable costs regardless of whether feasibility is shown, the research is ordinarily funded to the extent of the payments, consistent with Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Smith. Company-borne costs outside the award still require the allocation analysis in Section 4.
Phase II (R&D)
Greatest opportunity for partial claims on company-borne costs beyond the award.

Qualified; see Section 4. If the taxpayer retains substantial rights, funding reduces otherwise-qualified QREs, by default 100% against QREs. Costs above the grant are not automatically claimable on a dollar-for-dollar basis. In Smith (2026), the Tax Court required the taxpayer to show, project by project, that its QREs exceeded what the funder paid; only the excess was eligible.
Phase III (commercialization)
Post-production research excluded because it fails the "four-part test."

The exclusion is a separate statutory exclusion, §41(d)(4)(A): "Any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component." It is not part of the four-part test in §41(d)(1). See also Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(2). Phase III research that occurs before commercial production of the relevant business component is not excluded by §41(d)(4)(A), and because Phase III by definition uses non-SBIR/STTR money, it may be wholly self-funded or funded by a different party whose agreement must be tested separately.

body.text: 3.3 Keeping funded and self-funded work separate

KBKG's article supports the underlying point. Clear cost separation is its central recommendation, and it notes that any self-funded portion may remain eligible. It is consistent with the regulation, which applies the funding rules project by project (§1.41-4A(d)(3)(iii)), and with Smith, where the taxpayer's ability to claim anything on partially funded projects depended on proving excess expenses for each project.

Separation has two dimensions. Scope: research activities that the grant does not pay for and that the funder has no rights in may be a separate business component or project entirely, rather than an "excess" over the grant. Cost: within a single funded project, the business must be able to show its total research expenses, its otherwise-qualified expenses, and the funding received, because those are the inputs to the allocation rules in Section 4.
4. Allocating funding when research is only partly funded
4.1 The default rule

Where the taxpayer retains substantial rights, §1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) treats the research as funded to the extent of the payments received, plus the fair market value of any property received. Otherwise-qualified research expenses are reduced by that funding. The ATG explains that, unless the pro rata requirements are met, funding is allocated 100% to otherwise-qualified research expenses.

It is an accurate description of the outcome: under the default rule, every grant dollar is charged first against the expenses that would otherwise generate the credit, and only the QREs left over after the full grant has been absorbed remain creditable.
4.2 The pro rata exception and the 65% rule

Under §1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii), the taxpayer may allocate funding pro rata between non-qualified and otherwise-qualified expenses only if it can establish, to the satisfaction of the district director (the ATG says "the Service"; the district director position no longer exists, and the function now sits with the IRS), all three of the following:

items: the total amount of research expenses;
that total research expenses exceed the funding; and
that otherwise-qualified research expenses exceed 65 percent of the funding.

body.text: Even then, "In no event, however, shall less than 65 percent of the funding be applied against the otherwise qualified research expenses." Under §1.41-4A(d)(3)(iii), these rules are applied separately to each research project. The ATG notes that material adjustments may be warranted where the pro rata requirements are not met.

The 65% figure has two roles. It is an eligibility threshold (otherwise-qualified QREs must exceed 65% of funding), and it is a minimum on how much of the funding must be charged against QREs. The rule guarantees nothing to the taxpayer. It limits how far the pro rata method can shift funding away from QREs. The 65% figure in §1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) should also not be confused with the separate 65% rule in IRC §41(b)(3), which limits contract research expenses paid to third parties to 65% of the amount paid; the two rules operate independently.
4.3 Funding not yet known at filing

Under §1.41-4A(d)(5), if the amount of funding cannot be determined when the return is filed, the taxpayer treats the research as completely funded for that return. Once the funding is known, it should amend that return and any interim returns. Paragraph (d)(4) covers independent research and development and bid-and-proposal costs under federal contracts. This rule is especially relevant to multi-year grants, cost-share awards whose final reimbursable amount depends on a closeout audit, and awards that were interrupted by the 2025–2026 SBIR/STTR lapse.
4.4 Hypothetical worked example

Hypothetical. A company receives a $200,000 grant for a project. Payment is not contingent on success, and the company retains substantial rights. Total research expenses on the project are $500,000. Of that, $300,000 would be QREs absent funding.
Default method (100% allocation): $300,000 − $200,000 = $100,000 of QREs remain.
Pro rata method. First check eligibility:

items: Total expenses are established at $500,000.
$500,000 is greater than the $200,000 of funding.

body.text: All three conditions are met. Under a proportional reading (analysis: the regulation says "pro rata" without prescribing a formula), the QRE share of total expenses is $300,000 ÷ $500,000 = 60%. Funding charged to QREs would be 60% × $200,000 = $120,000.
That is below the 65% minimum of $130,000, so $130,000 must be applied. QREs remaining: $300,000 − $130,000 = $170,000.

The difference between the two methods in this example is $70,000 of QREs, which illustrates why the documentation needed to satisfy the three pro rata conditions (Section 6.3) has real value for grant recipients.
Only otherwise-qualified expenses can be QREs, and the regulation dictates how funding is charged against them.
4.5 Scenario table

cells: Guaranteed (fixed-fee) payment; IP retained by client
100% funding allocation (default); excluded

Excluded, but because of §1.41-4A(d)(2): no substantial rights means fully funded. The 100% allocation default under (d)(3) applies only where rights are retained. See Tangel, Grigsby, and the two no-rights projects in Smith.
Cost-share grant with documented overruns; taxpayer keeps IP
Attempt pro rata (65% rule); partially qualified
Consistent with §1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)–(ii), if all three pro rata conditions are proven for that project. Without that proof, the 100% default applies and only QREs exceeding the funding remain.
"Fee contingent on success (Time & Materials)"; taxpayer keeps IP
0% funding allocation; 100% qualified

Success-contingent payments are not funding under (d)(1). Time-and-materials billing is ordinarily not success-contingent, so it should not be used as the example. Under Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Smith, the contingency must appear expressly or by clear implication in the agreement. The expenses must still pass the other §41 requirements.
Grant amount unknown at filing
Treat as completely funded; amend later
The citation is §1.41-4A(d)(5).

body.text: 5. Other funding types (analysis)

items: State grants and vouchers are treated like federal grants for this purpose. This is consistent with the statute's reference to any "governmental entity," which is not limited to the federal government.
Equity investment and repayable loans are not "funded research."
Forgivable loans may effectively become grants.

body.text: The only related item found is ADP's statement that, for Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans, qualified R&D wages may need to be reduced by the forgiven amount.

As an analytical matter (not a verified rule), the regulation's focus on agreements with "other persons" and on whether amounts paid are contingent on research success suggests that the label on a financing instrument is not decisive. What matters is whether another party is paying for the research under terms that leave the taxpayer without the risk of failure or without substantial rights. Taxpayers with unusual funding structures should test them against §1.41-4A(d) directly.
6. Documentation and audit exposure for grant-funded claims
6.1 The audit environment (commentary)

DST Advisory Group (September 2, 2025) expects fewer IRS audits overall but R&D audits that are more intense and detailed. It also expects the IRS to rely more on taxpayer-provided information, and it warns that incomplete, disorganized, or poorly substantiated claims will be red flags. This is the firm's own analysis, not IRS statistics. KBKG warns that ignoring funding sources can lead to overstated credits and potential audit penalties, without specifying penalty rules.

The case law confirms that funded research is a live audit and litigation issue. The IRS has litigated the exclusion repeatedly and prevailed in Tangel (2021), Grigsby (2023), Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (2024), and, on the funded projects, Smith (2026). In several of these cases the issue was decided on summary judgment, purely from the contract terms, without the court reaching the technical merits of the research.
6.2 Form 6765 and the Harper case

Form 6765 is titled "Credit for Increasing Research Activities" (IRS). The IRS instructions (Rev. 12/2025, applying to the January 2025 revision of the form) list "Research funded by another person (or governmental entity)" as an excluded activity. For tax years beginning before 2026, Section G (business component information) is optional. For tax years beginning after 2025 it is required, unless an exception applies. The exceptions are: a qualified small business under §41(h)(3) that checks the box to claim the reduced payroll tax credit; and a filer reporting the credit on an original return whose total QREs at the controlled-group level are $1.5 million or less and whose average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less. The instructions also state that the maximum amount a qualified small business can apply against payroll tax is $500,000.

For grant recipients, the practical effect of Section G is that funded and partially funded business components must be identified and reported at the component level on returns for tax years beginning in 2026 and later (unless an exception applies), which makes the separation of funded and self-funded work described in Section 3.3 a filing requirement as well as an audit-defense practice.

The case is Harper v. United States, No. 19-55933, 847 Fed. App'x 408 (9th Cir. Feb. 25, 2021) (unpublished), which reversed the district court's dismissal (S.D. Cal., No. 3:18-cv-02110). The Ninth Circuit held that the IRS's lengthy, substantive examination of the refund claim over a four-year audit, followed by denial on the merits, waived the IRS's enforcement of the refund-claim specificity requirement, and it remanded the case. The case therefore shows the procedural risk a claim faces, but the taxpayer won on that issue. Because the decision is unpublished, it is not binding precedent even within the Ninth Circuit.
6.3 Records that separate funded from self-funded work

items: Labor. Systems for time tracking, project codes, and indirect cost allocation are needed to separate qualified from non-qualified work (The Tax Adviser, October 2025). R&D planning also requires collaboration across finance, engineering, and operations.

Contemporaneous evidence. Useful records include iterations of design specifications and engineering drawings, internal presentations and meeting notes, test data, and records of failures. QREs can be supported with time sheets and supply invoices that connect the cost to the activity (The Tax Adviser, July 2016).

Agreement file. For each funded project, a complete copy of the grant or contract documents, including incorporated terms and any data-rights or IP clauses, should be kept with the credit workpapers. The decisions in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Grigsby, Tangel, and Smith each turned on the text of those documents.

Funding trail (analysis). For grant-funded projects, the same records should show which costs were reimbursed by the grant and which were borne by the company. Without that trail, the three facts needed for the pro rata method in Section 4.2 cannot be established, the 100% default applies, and, as Smith illustrates, the taxpayer may be unable to prove that any QREs exceeded the funding at all.

body.text: 8. Conclusion
A grant does not disqualify a business from the research credit. The rules are:

items: Research is excluded "to the extent" it is funded (IRC §41(d)(4)(H)).
Research is fully funded if the business keeps no substantial rights (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d)(2)).

Payments contingent on success are not funding (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d)(1)), but courts require that contingency to appear expressly or by clear implication in the agreement; general business risk, fixed prices, or progress-based payments are not enough (Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, 8th Cir. 2024; Grigsby, 5th Cir. 2023; Smith, T.C. Memo. 2026-50).

Where rights are retained, funding reduces otherwise-qualified QREs, by default dollar-for-dollar. A pro rata method is available only if the business proves total expenses, that expenses exceed funding, and that QREs exceed 65% of funding, and at least 65% of the funding must still be charged against QREs. These rules apply project by project.
If the funding amount is unknown at filing, the research is treated as fully funded until the return is amended (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d)(5)).

The funded-research regulations remain in force after Loper Bright (Smith, 2026), and SBIR/STTR awards, which resumed after the programs were reauthorized through September 30, 2031 by Pub. L. 119-83, remain subject to these same rules.

body.text: The practical result depends on the wording of the grant agreement and on records that separate funded from self-funded costs. For tax years beginning after 2025, those records also feed the business-component reporting required in Section G of Form 6765 for most filers.
